title: The issue with Novice Programs
summary: NH criticizes popular novice programs such as Starting Strength: they are powerlifting-centric, obsessed with fast progression on the Big 3, built on static rep schemes that cause plateaus, lacking isolation and diversity, idolized with cult followings, and they push dirty bulks like GOMAD. His alternative gives novices less frequency, more movement patterns including isolation, evolving rep schemes and maintenance-level eating so they stay in the game long term and learn to program.
claims: Novice programs matter because they are lifters' first exposure to structured programming and discipline
NH used to go to the gym and do whatever: random machines one day, bench another; he never adapted neurologically to lifts and never progressed
Compound movements are the best for hypertrophy and strength, but you can't build a program from only compounds
Novices should come in, do two to three movements and go home rather than spend two hours in the gym
About 75% of the time, a novice asking for a program online is told Starting Strength
Roughly 90% of YouTube fitness viewers are novices, with high turnover; some people stay novices for five years by quitting and restarting
Naming programs after yourself creates cult followings that credit the creator for gains novices would have made on anything
Because everything works for novices, we should choose what novices do based on long-term criteria, not results alone
Millions using a program reflects seniority, not quality
Novice programs are obsessed with progression and turn training into a race to stack plates
Going from a 60 lb to a 200 lb squat in the first year is a given, not an accomplishment
Noob gains are not a window that closes in hours; they represent a certain amount of development, and you can ride them for years
The goal is not to be strongest fastest but to stick with it the longest
Highly repetitive Big 3 programs cause a lot of injuries in novices
NH trains high-bar squat, standard bench and close-stance conventional deadlift because they fit his build, not because everyone should
Tall lifters may suit dips, low-bar squats or sumo instead; the program should adapt to the lifter, not vice versa
Starting Strength is designed to hit plateaus quickly, because plateaus are treated as the signal to become intermediate
5x5, 3x5 and 3x3 are static rep schemes; repeating 5x5 requires a PR on five sets at once, which stops working once noob gains end
Early plateaus come from not having accumulated quality volume beforehand
Lowering the weight and redoing the same linear progression is why many people quit
If you train 20 years you'll be a novice about six months; stretching it to a year costs nothing and builds good habits
Size and strength standards (e.g. full-plate deadlift) are worthless and promote rushing with bad form
Enjoy the novice stage like childhood; you'll be intermediate soon enough
GOMAD is a garbage way to get macros even for very skinny guys and promotes unaesthetic, fat weight gain that can cause body dysmorphia
NH's programs are at least 80% compound movements, but novices don't need to squat or bench three times a week
Novice programs lack curls, triceps extensions, calf, neck, forearm and direct ab work, and GPP
Cutting ~20% of the Big 3 volume to add diversity would make programs better and less boring
Training only bench, squat and deadlift wasn't great for hypertrophy and became boring for NH
NH's novice program squats once or twice a week and deadlifts once a week
A novice squatting twice a week will be more consistent long term and outlast one squatting three times
Give novices just enough to keep them interested and hungry to come back
NH's first sessions were 20 minutes of push-ups, sit-ups and air squats; more would have burnt him out
Deadlifting once a week makes novices excited to return for a PR and less likely to skip
Weight jumps and the frequency of adding weight shrink exponentially over a career, so slowing early progression can extend it
Gaining 200 lb on your squat while also gaining a lot of bodyweight is worthless
Novices benefit most from maintenance calories, slowly increasing as appetite grows; a 500+ kcal surplus is a waste
NH programs novices 'building-centric': more movement patterns like curls, delaying bench plateaus by months while gaining more total volume
Compound lifts belong to bodybuilders too; 1950s bodybuilders used them before powerlifting existed
A 2-rep max deadlift done for hypertrophy purposes is hypertrophy training; strength and size are intertwined
Most people start lifting for aesthetics but novice programs groom them into powerlifters
Many 'failed powerlifters' were funneled into strength early, resent people who look good, and are among the most toxic in fitness
Most novices never reach intermediate because of injuries, plateaus and boredom, not just personal failings
Novice programs forbid modification, so lifters never learn to program and struggle at the intermediate transition
A novice program modified with evolving rep schemes, variations and rotations would carry you through the intermediate stage
